label: Virtue ethics
description: Morality centres on character: the stable dispositions (virtues) that make a human life go well, cultivated through habit and practical wisdom.
assumptions: Humans have a characteristic flourishing (eudaimonia)
Character is formed by habituation
Practical wisdom cannot be reduced to rules

label: Utilitarianism
description: The right action is the one that produces the best overall consequences, usually understood as the greatest balance of well-being for everyone affected.
assumptions: Well-being can be compared and aggregated across people
Each person's interests count equally
Consequences are what ultimately matter morally

label: Kantian deontology
description: Morality is a matter of duty grounded in reason: act only on principles you could will as universal law and treat persons always as ends, never merely as means.
assumptions: Rational agents are bound by the moral law
Persons have dignity, not a price
Good outcomes cannot justify using people

label: Stoicism
description: A good life consists in virtue and in correctly distinguishing what is up to us (judgements, choices) from what is not, accepting the latter with equanimity.
assumptions: Only virtue is truly good
Distress comes from judgements, not events
Nature is rationally ordered

label: Epicureanism
description: The goal of life is pleasure understood as tranquillity: freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance, reached through simple living, friendship and understanding nature.
assumptions: Pleasure is the natural good
Many desires are unnecessary
Fear of death and the gods is unfounded

label: Confucian role ethics
description: Moral life is cultivated within relationships and roles through ritual propriety (li), humaneness (ren) and learning, aiming at harmony in family and society.
assumptions: Persons are constituted by relationships
Ritual shapes character
Good government rests on virtue more than law

label: Hobbesian social contract
description: Without a common power people live in a war of all against all; rational individuals therefore authorize a strong sovereign to secure peace.
assumptions: Humans are roughly equal and self-interested
Security is the precondition of every other good
Authority derives from consent motivated by fear

label: Liberal individualism
description: Individuals possess rights and a sphere of liberty that government exists to protect; freedom means acting on one's own choices without coercion as long as others are not harmed.
assumptions: Individuals are the primary unit of moral concern
Legitimate power requires consent and limits
Freedom is chiefly freedom from interference

label: Civic republicanism
description: Freedom is realized through participation in self-government and the absence of domination; citizens share a common good that politics must express.
assumptions: Political participation is part of a free life
Dependence on another's will is unfreedom
A public realm must be actively sustained

label: Egalitarian liberalism
description: A just society secures equal basic liberties and arranges social and economic inequalities so that they benefit the least advantaged.
assumptions: Natural and social luck is morally arbitrary
Principles of justice are those chosen impartially
Fair institutions matter more than individual charity

label: Market liberalism
description: Free exchange, private property and spontaneous order coordinate dispersed knowledge better than central planning; coercive redistribution threatens liberty.
assumptions: Knowledge is dispersed and cannot be centralized
Voluntary exchange tends to be mutually beneficial
Concentrated power is the main threat to freedom

label: Marxist critique
description: Social life is shaped by material production and class relations; under capitalism workers are alienated and exploited, and ideas often serve dominant interests.
assumptions: Economic structure shapes institutions and ideas
History moves through class conflict
Labour is central to human self-realization

label: Existentialism
description: Human beings have no fixed essence; we are radically free and responsible for what we make of ourselves, and evading that freedom is bad faith.
assumptions: Existence precedes essence
Freedom cannot be escaped
Meaning is created, not given

label: Religious existentialism
description: The individual stands before God and must choose with passionate inwardness; rational systems, crowds and promises of comfortable happiness cannot replace that personal commitment.
assumptions: Truth for a life is lived subjectively
Freedom includes the capacity to reject reason's plans
Faith exceeds what reason can prove

label: Genealogical critique
description: Moral values have a history rooted in psychology and power; inherited morality should be questioned by asking what kinds of life it expresses and promotes.
assumptions: Values are human creations with histories
Moral judgements can mask resentment or power
Self-overcoming matters more than comfort

label: Technological criticism
description: Technology is not a neutral tool: it reshapes how we perceive the world, ourselves and our capacities, and can turn everything — including people — into resources to be optimized.
assumptions: Tools change their users
Efficiency is not a neutral value
What technology reveals can also conceal

label: Scientific empiricism
description: Knowledge claims must answer to experience and evidence; conclusions should be proportioned to the evidence and held open to revision.
assumptions: Experience is the basis of factual knowledge
Claims should be testable
Certainty about matters of fact is unavailable

label: Critical rationalism
description: We learn by bold conjecture and attempted refutation; scientific theories must be falsifiable, and open societies institutionalize criticism.
assumptions: Theories cannot be verified, only corroborated or refuted
Criticism is the engine of progress
Utopian planning tends toward closed societies

label: Paradigm theory of science
description: Science develops through paradigms that structure normal research until anomalies accumulate and revolutions replace them; rival paradigms are not simply compared by neutral rules.
assumptions: Scientific practice is shaped by shared exemplars
Observation is theory-laden
Paradigm change is not purely logical

label: Feminist philosophy
description: Gendered hierarchies are social constructions sustained by education, institutions and ideas; freedom and reason must be secured for women as fully as for men.
assumptions: Many differences attributed to nature are produced socially
Dependence and lack of education produce subordination
Universal claims can hide a particular point of view

label: Psychoanalysis
description: Much of mental life is unconscious; civilization demands the renunciation and redirection of instinctual drives, which produces both culture and discontent.
assumptions: Unconscious drives shape behaviour
Civilization requires repression or sublimation of instincts
Self-understanding requires interpreting hidden motives

label: Capabilities approach
description: Well-being and justice should be assessed by people's real freedoms — what they are actually able to do and be — rather than by income or utility alone.
assumptions: Resources convert into freedoms differently for different people
Development means expanding substantive freedoms
Public reasoning should choose priorities

label: Platonic rationalism
description: True knowledge grasps unchanging forms beyond appearances; the soul and the city are just when reason rules, and opinion or persuasion is not wisdom.
assumptions: Appearances differ from reality
Knowledge differs from mere opinion
Those who know should guide those who do not
